Maintaining the dataset manifest

Source: SKILL.md

Scope note (datazoom.saude). This file was adapted from the sibling package datazoom.amazonia, which uses the same manifest architecture. The rules below apply to this package as written, but many worked examples (MapBiomas, PRODES, DETER, DEGRAD, ANEEL, EPE, IPS, SEEG and their resolve_*.R / R/*.R files) are historical incidents from datazoom.amazonia and do not exist in this repository. Here the resolvers are actions/scrapers/resolve_datasus.R and actions/scrapers/resolve_sipni.R, and the manifest is fetched from the main branch.

Every download URL this package uses lives in one CSV — inst/extdata/manifest/v1/datasets_link.csv — fetched fresh at runtime with a silent fallback to the packaged snapshot. A scheduled robot (actions/scripts/build_manifest.R, run by .github/workflows/update-manifest.yaml) proposes updates; nothing is ever auto-committed; every change becomes a pull request for a human to review.

Read this whole file before touching any of these paths. It assumes zero memory of how this system was built — only what it looks like today.

What goes in NEWS.md vs. this file

NEWS.md is for the package’s users: load_<source>()’s output changed, a bug that affected what it returns got fixed, a dataset was added or removed. It is not a running log of internal maintenance work – a new resolver’s verification technique, the exact wording of a # FRAGILE: tag, or an architectural decision belongs here (this file), not there. A finding that doesn’t change what the package ships right now (a known bug not yet fixed, an evaluated-but-rejected option) belongs in this file’s “Known limitations” section and/or a GitHub Issue, never in NEWS.md as if it were a change. (2026-10-12: several existing NEWS.md entries, including DETER’s and ANEEL’s, currently carry more internal detail than this rule says they should – a cleanup is planned but hasn’t happened yet; don’t take their current length/detail as the pattern to copy for a new entry.)

Before opening a PR

Two mechanical checks, easy to lose track of in the middle of a real fix, that have already bitten this project at least once each:

  • Run the devtools round-trip before opening the PR, not just before committing R/ changes. devtools::load_all() then devtools::document() (plus whatever else the local workflow normally runs, e.g. devtools::check()) regenerates man/*.Rd, NAMESPACE, and any other roxygen-derived metadata from the current state of R/. A new or renamed exported function, a changed @param, or a new @importFrom only reaches those generated files through this step — editing R/*.R alone leaves them silently stale, and nothing short of actually running it catches that before a reviewer does.
  • A new call to another package’s function from R/*.R means that package must be added to DESCRIPTION’s Imports:, in the same commit. Easy to lose track of when the function is pulled in as a side effect of a larger change rather than the point of it — e.g. R/balanca_tls.R’s TLS fallback (2026-10-21) needed curl::new_handle()/curl::curl_download(), so curl was added to Imports: alongside it, even though curl was already on disk as a transitive dependency of googledrive — being installed already does not make a package an Imports: dependency, only a DESCRIPTION entry does, and R CMD check’s “undeclared dependency” check is what actually catches a miss, not whether the package happens to load fine during development. This is for R/ only — a dependency used only inside actions/ (a resolver, a watcher, a build script) stays out of DESCRIPTION entirely, since that whole directory is .Rbuildignored and never ships to a package user (see point 6 under “Writing a new resolver” below — jsonlite, used by some resolvers, is correctly CI-only and absent from Imports:). Don’t add a package to DESCRIPTION by reflex just because its name is new in a diff — check first whether the call is in R/ or actions/.

The one rule everything else follows from

Every manifest row is self-sufficient. A row carries every value a lookup might need for it, explicitly, even if that means repeating a value that’s identical on a sibling row. A blank cell means this field genuinely has no value for this row — never “look at another row instead.”

There is no inheritance, no tiering, and — since 2026-08-19 — no base row either. This replaced an earlier 5-tier field-coalescing design (survey default → dataset → geo_level/year overrides), then a self-sufficient-rows design that kept every dataset’s own blank-key “base row” alongside its real overrides. Both migrations were chasing the same bug shape: two rows of one dataset silently disagreeing about a value because only one of them was ever asked. The base row turned out to be just as capable of this as the tiers it replaced — a live example: mapbiomas_mining’s committed base row stayed pinned to Collection 8 for weeks after both its real override rows had already moved to Collection 9 (see NEWS.md). If you ever find yourself writing code that reads a value from one row to decide what another row should imply, stop — that is the exact pattern both migrations removed. Every row answers for itself.

Concretely, this means:

  • dataset is never NA. There is no more “survey-default” row. If a value is shared by every dataset in a source, it is copied onto every one of that source’s rows, redundantly, on purpose.
  • A (survey, dataset) group is either UNKEYED (exactly one row, geo_level and year both blank — that one row IS the dataset) or KEYED (every row carries a real geo_level XOR year — no blank-key row at all). Never both. There is no more “base row + overrides” — a keyed dataset’s rows must each carry a full, independent copy of everything they need, not just what differs from a row that no longer exists.
  • A dataset never mixes geo_level overrides and year overrides. Pick one axis of variation per dataset (enforced by tests/testthat/test-manifest-schema.R and actions/scripts/manifest_validate.R’s validate_key_completeness()).
  • If a keyed dataset varies by geo_level, every value its rows agree on in available_geo must have a matching row, and every row that exists must be declared there — both directions checked (same for year / available_time). There is no fallback left to catch a missing one — a lookup for a geo_level/year with no matching row returns NA, full stop.

How a lookup resolves (R/manifest.R)

Two different functions now, deliberately kept separate so nothing has to guess which row “wins”:

dataset_field(source, dataset, field, geo_level = NULL, year = NULL)

is a single exact-key match, not a search:

  1. If the dataset has any geo_level-specific rows, match geo_level exactly — and if the caller passed none, stop(). There is no base row left to fall back to.
  2. Else if it has any year-specific rows, match year exactly — same stop() if the caller passed none.
  3. Else (the dataset is unkeyed) use its one real row, ignoring whatever geo_level/year the caller may have passed anyway (callers pass these unconditionally — see R/mapbiomas.R’s sheet lookup, which passes geo_level even for unkeyed datasets like mapbiomas_fire).
  4. Read field off that ONE row. Return its value, even if that value is NA.

dataset_url() is dataset_field(..., "url", ...).

dataset_meta(source, dataset, field)

is the one legal cross-row read, for a field in MANIFEST_META_COLS (sidra_code, available_time, available_geo, layer_name, resolver — notably not url, docs_url, or version: several MapBiomas datasets deliberately pin one geo_level to an older Dataverse collection than its siblings, so those two genuinely vary per row now, permanently, not as a bug — see that constant’s comment in R/manifest.R). Returns the single value every row of the dataset agrees on; stop()s if they disagree — it cannot silently pick a winner, which is exactly why it can’t reproduce the old base-row bug. If you hit that error, the field isn’t safe to read without a key for that dataset — use dataset_field() with a real key instead (see R/mapbiomas.R’s version lookup for a worked example of exactly this call getting keyed instead of migrated to dataset_meta(), once real per-row divergence was found).

effective_table() (what datasets_link() exposes) synthesizes ONE display row per (survey, dataset) by collapsing every value column to “the value every row agrees on, else NA” — the same collapse dataset_meta() does, just silently NA’d instead of thrown, since building the whole display table can’t crash over one dataset’s expected divergence. A NA here does not mean “no data” — it can mean “this genuinely differs by geo_level/year, ask dataset_field() for a specific one” (mapbiomas_cover’s url, for example). Override rows are only ever reachable through dataset_field()/ dataset_meta(), never through effective_table()/datasets_link().

The manifest’s 14 columns

survey, dataset, geo_level, year (key) · sidra_code, url, docs_url, available_time, available_geo, archive_file, sheet, layer_name, version, resolver (value). Full description of each: see the header comment of R/manifest.R and the table in the published artifact guide (ask the user for the link if you need it — it isn’t stored in the repo).

resolver names which resolve_<source>.R owns a row. Blank means no robot ever touches it — hand-maintained permanently (e.g. Google Drive links with no discoverable version).

Writing a new resolver

File: actions/scrapers/resolve_<source>.R, function resolve_<source>(rows). Auto-discovered by build_manifest.R via filename convention — there is no registry to edit.

  1. Investigate the source manually first, in a browser, before writing any code. Figure out the actual mechanism: a documented API the site’s own page calls client-side (preferred — see resolve_prodes.R, resolve_aneel.R), a bucket-listing API (resolve_mapbiomas.R’s GCS half), URL probing for a version stamp (resolve_baci.R), or, only if nothing else exists, real HTML scraping (resolve_mapbiomas.R’s WordPress half). Record what you verified live and when, in the file’s header comment — every existing resolver does this; it’s how the next person avoids re-investigating from scratch when the site changes shape again.

  2. rows is the manifest rows currently tagged resolver == "<source>". Most resolvers ignore its contents and re-discover everything from the network, but you MUST use it to know which dataset/geo_level rows to fan a shared value across — this is the part that’s easy to get wrong. If one URL or version applies to every real row of a dataset (or to every dataset a source owns), emit one row per key, not just one shared row — and only for keys that actually exist as rows today (see point 3 below; there is no base row to also write anymore):

    # WRONG — under self-sufficient rows this leaves siblings stale
tibble(survey = "x", dataset = NA_character_, url = found_url)

# ALSO WRONG for a keyed dataset — geo_level = NA_character_ here would
# try to match/create a blank-key row, which no longer exists; it would
# bind_rows() a brand-new, duplicate row instead of updating anything
# (this exact bug was found live in resolve_mapbiomas.R's configs before
# the base-row-deletion migration -- see that file's header)
tibble(survey = "x", dataset = "keyed_dataset", geo_level = NA_character_, url = found_url)

# RIGHT — fan out across every REAL row this resolver owns
tibble(survey = "x", dataset = unique(rows$dataset), url = found_url)

    See resolve_prodes.R/resolve_seeg.R/resolve_ips.R for “fan across every dataset a source owns,” and resolve_epe.R/resolve_mapbiomas.R for “fan across every geo_level row of one dataset” (resolve_epe.R’s consumer/industrial-consumption block reads rows$geo_level directly rather than hardcoding a geo_level list — that pattern automatically adapts if a dataset’s real key set ever changes, prefer it over a hardcoded vector like resolve_mapbiomas.R’s configs list uses).

  3. Never target dataset = NA, and never emit a blank-key (geo_level/year both NA) row for a dataset that has real override rows. Neither row type exists anymore; the candidate will fail validate_row_grouping() for real, immediately (see actions/scripts/manifest_validate.R).

  4. Return only the columns you want to change. NA in a returned column means “leave whatever is already there alone” — it is not “clear this field.” (This is enforced downstream by build_manifest.R’s non_na_cols guard, but don’t rely on it to save you from a resolver that dplyr::bind_rows()s differently-shaped sub-tibbles together and accidentally NA-pads a column it never meant to touch — check what your own bind_rows() call actually produces before returning it.)

  5. stop() on any real failure. Never return a partial or guessed result. A thrown error just leaves that source’s rows untouched for this run and gets reported by name (resolvers_failed in the JSON report, exit code 30) — it does not fail the other resolvers or corrupt anything.

    Exception — a resolver covering several independent sub-sources. resolve_epe.R covers 3 unrelated pages (consumo-mensal, BEN Anexo IX, BEN Chapter 8) in one function. A single stop() at the end (only when all sub-sources fail) has a real gap: one sub-source silently failing while the others succeed produces no error at all — no resolvers_failed entry, no PR, no issue — and the affected row(s) just go stale with zero visibility. Confirmed live: this is very likely how energy_state_panel’s dead URL persisted undetected for as long as it did (see NEWS.md). The fix, now the pattern to follow for any resolver with more than one sub-source: track each sub-source’s own failure reason (a block_failures <- character(0) accumulator is fine), still stop() only when every sub-source fails, but if some succeeded and some didn’t, return the successful rows normally (never discard them — that would reintroduce the exact “one broken thing blocks everyone else” bug the resolver-level exit-code-11 machinery exists to prevent) with the failure reasons attached as attr(result, "partial_failures") — build_manifest.R reads that attribute, reports it as resolvers_partial_failed in the JSON report, and folds its length into total_failed so it still trips exit code 11 (changes + a failure) instead of looking like a clean run. See resolve_epe.R’s header and build_manifest.R’s resolver_partial_failed handling for the working example — verified live by forcing one of its three blocks to fail and confirming the other two still merged while the failure surfaced (exit code 30, resolvers_partial_failed: {"epe": "..."}), then reverting the forced failure. Also applied to resolve_mapbiomas.R (its ~10-config loop had the identical gap one layer further down — dv_get_json() silently swallowed a transport/parse failure into an empty result, indistinguishable from a config that genuinely found no new candidate; it now throws instead, letting the failure reach the same per-config tryCatch) — same live-verified-by-forcing-a-failure discipline, see that file’s own header for the specifics.

    A second, successful-but-noteworthy sibling: fallback_notes. partial_failures signals something that didn’t resolve; a resolver can also succeed through a looser, still-safe path than its usual precise one (e.g. resolve_deter.R’s keyword fallback when a known TerraBrasilis slug disappears and a single unambiguous match is found by the dataset’s human-readable name instead, with every already-claimed or ambiguous candidate excluded). That is a completely normal success, not a failure, and must NEVER trip resolver_failed/resolver_partial_failed or affect the exit code. Attach attr(result, "fallback_notes") (a character vector) instead — build_manifest.R reads it into resolver_fallback_notes and adds a dedicated PR-body section naming exactly which value(s) came from the fallback, so a human reviewer knows to look closer before merging. Added 2026-10-08 alongside resolve_deter.R’s fallback: before this existed, the only trace of a fallback firing was a message() that reached the CI log, never the PR body a human actually reads. See resolve_deter.R’s header and tests/testthat/test-deter-resolver.R for the worked example, including the guard (a link another dataset’s known slug still claims is never a candidate here, and two datasets resolving to the same URL is always a hard stop()) that keeps the fallback from ever picking an ambiguous or wrongly-shared candidate.

  6. CI-only dependencies are fine here (curl, jsonlite, stringr) — actions/ is .Rbuildignored. Never add them to DESCRIPTION’s Imports.

  7. If the source has a genuinely newer file the package can’t read yet (a different sheet layout, a different column range), do not push that URL — see “Detect-only resolvers” below.

Verifying a candidate: the sheet name is not enough either

resolve_mapbiomas.R’s own header states the first half of this rule: “a 200 response is not enough, verify the sheet is really there.” There’s a sequel worth stating just as explicitly: a matching sheet name isn’t enough either — the sheet has to have the columns the treatment code actually needs. Live incident: Dataverse’s newest “Collection 10.1” cover/municipality dataset has a sheet named exactly right (COVERAGE_10.1, matches sheet_pattern = "^COVERAGE") but no municipality-code column anywhere in it — a resolver that only checked the sheet name would have silently served that file with no way to look up a municipality. resolve_mapbiomas.R’s dv_file_layout() now also downloads the sheet’s real header row and takes an optional required_col_pattern; a candidate that matches the sheet name but not the required column is treated exactly like a sheet-name mismatch — the newest-first walk falls through to the next-older candidate, self-healing onto whatever collection next actually has the column, no hardcoded version number anywhere. Give a config a required_col_pattern whenever the treatment code has a real, specific column dependency on that row (not just “some sheet with a plausible name”) — see resolve_mapbiomas.R’s mapbiomas_cover/municipality config for the pattern.

Detect-only resolvers

A detect-only resolver is the pattern for “found a newer file, but the loader doesn’t match its layout yet.” It emits only version + docs_url, never url — say so explicitly in the header comment. Pushing a URL the package isn’t ready to read would corrupt every download until someone fixes the loader, silently. Follow this pattern for any source in the same situation.

resolve_seeg.R USED TO be this category’s canonical example, on an assumption (“the live municipal-summary workbook is a different shape” than R/seeg.R’s expected NIVEL 1..NIVEL 6 layout) that was never actually checked. 2026-09-15: checked it, live — the assumption was TRUE, and worse than the resolver’s header guessed (a full schema restructuring, not a version bump). It now emits a real url, re-verified every run via a ranged GET of the candidate xlsx’s own xl/workbook.xml and xl/pivotCache/pivotCacheDefinition1.xml, and R/seeg.R was rewritten sector by sector against the new schema (see NEWS.md). Same lesson as IPS below, learned twice now: verify a “different shape” assumption live before committing to detect-only, not after.

resolve_ips.R USED TO be detect-only too, on an assumption (the Strapi-hosted workbook it finds is “a different shape” than R/ips.R’s expected layout) that was never actually checked. 2026-09-14: checked it, live — the two workbooks are a drop-in match (same sheets, row counts, cleaned column names) — so it now emits a real url, re-verified every run via a ranged GET of the workbook’s own xl/workbook.xml (an xlsx is a zip; see zip_remote_listing.R) rather than trusted from that one-time comparison. Lesson for the next detect-only resolver: the “different shape” assumption is exactly the kind of thing to verify live before committing to detect-only, not after.

R gotchas that have already bitten this codebase once

  • tibble() argument shadowing: tibble() evaluates arguments left to right, and a later argument can reference an earlier one by column name. If you write tibble(year = NA_character_, available_time = year) meaning to reference an outer variable called year, you’ll silently get the column you just defined instead. Rename the outer variable (release_year, not year) if it shares a name with any manifest column.
  • dplyr::bind_rows() of differently-shaped tibbles pads missing columns with NA on every row that lacked them. Downstream code reads that NA as “leave this alone” (see point 4 above) — which is what saves you, but only if you don’t also explicitly set that column to something wrong elsewhere in the same bind.
  • A short download timeout can silently corrupt a resolver’s verdict, not just fail loudly. If a resolver downloads a real file to verify it (see the sheet/column verification above), give the download a generous timeout — curl’s timeout handle option is a whole-transfer ceiling, not a stall detector, and on a slow connection a large candidate genuinely cannot finish inside a short one. Live incident: dv_file_layout() used timeout = 120; a legitimate 78MB candidate timed out at 43MB and was silently read as “doesn’t qualify” (no error raised, no failure logged), which cascaded the newest-first walk down to a much older, wrong file. Raised to 1000, matching the timeout R/download.R’s own external_download() already uses for its big downloads — match that convention for any new resolver that downloads real files to verify, don’t invent a tighter one.
  • A download failure must never look like “this candidate doesn’t qualify.” The bug above has a root cause worth generalizing: any tryCatch(..., error = function(e) NULL) around a network call, if NULL also means “sheet/column didn’t match,” conflates “we don’t know” with “we checked and it’s not right” — and a newest-first walk will treat both the same, silently falling through to a worse candidate on a transient hiccup. If a resolver has this shape, make the network failure stop() instead of returning the same sentinel a real content mismatch returns — it should propagate to the per-cfg/per-source tryCatch that already leaves a row untouched on error (see resolve_mapbiomas.R’s resolve_via_dataverse() for the pattern: a genuine sheet/column mismatch returns NULL and the walk continues; a download failure stop()s and the walk aborts for that config only, leaving its row exactly as it was).
  • manifest_url() defaults to GitHub’s main branch, not whatever branch your local checkout is on. devtools::load_all(".") loads your local R code, but load_mapbiomas() (and every other loader) still fetches the manifest from main at runtime unless you also set options(datazoom.saude.use_remote_manifest = FALSE) — these are two independent things, loading local code doesn’t imply reading the local manifest. Live confusion this caused: load_mapbiomas(dataset = "mapbiomas_cover", geo_level = "municipality") returned a stale sheet version because the remote fetch silently pulled master’s manifest (which had none of this branch’s fixes) instead of the local, already- correct file. Always set both options together when testing against local manifest edits.
  • An assumption about an OLDER collection’s shape needs live verification just as much as a new one. A # FRAGILE: comment in R/mapbiomas.R assumed Collection 9’s transition columns used a from_level_N/ to_level_N PREFIX (distinct from Collection 10’s confirmed class_level_N_from/_to SUFFIX) — turned out false. Live-verified by streaming just the header row of the real 606MB Collection 9 GCS file via HTTP range requests (see the technique note below) instead of trusting the comment: Collection 9 uses the exact same suffixed shape. The pt-language rename rule that assumed the prefix form had been silently matching zero columns since long before Collection 10 existed, not “broken by the migration” as the comment implied. Don’t inherit an unverified assumption about what an old, working collection looks like just because it predates the thing you’re actually changing.
  • Roxygen docs drift out of sync with the manifest silently — nothing enforces they stay matched. devtools::check() doesn’t catch a doc that merely under-states valid options. Live incident: mapbiomas_cover’s @param geo_level said “can only be municipality” for the entire time an indigenous_land manifest row existed (added during the Dataverse migration, §12 in the published migration artifact). Whenever a keyed dataset’s set of geo_level/year override rows changes, grep the corresponding load_<source>() roxygen block for a stale claim — don’t assume it was updated alongside the manifest just because they usually should move together.
  • Closures nested inside resolve_<source>(rows) cannot be unit-tested by mocking. dv_file_layout(), resolve_via_dataverse(), and similar helpers are typically defined inside the outer resolver function, not at file scope — there’s no accessible binding for testthat::local_mocked_bindings() (or any binding-replacement mock) to intercept, since the call never leaves that function’s own local environment. Don’t spend time trying; pull out only the pieces that genuinely need no network (see mapbiomas_resolver_cache.R’s cache_lookup()/cache_upsert()/rules_fingerprint() for what is extractable and worth unit-testing) and verify the network-touching parts by actually running them live, cold and warm, and diffing the output — see “Verifying any change” above and the resolver cache section below. (Counter-example worth knowing: resolve_deter.R’s keyword fallback is a plain top-level function — not a closure captured inside a bigger helper — specifically so test-deter-resolver.R can mock curl at the package-function level, via testthat::with_mocked_bindings(), and exercise the fallback offline against a real-shaped fixture. Prefer a flat, mockable shape like this over a nested closure whenever a resolver’s matching logic is complex enough to deserve its own regression tests.)
  • dplyr::recode() (and anything built on it, like rename_with(recode, ...)) treats an unmatched name or value as “leave it exactly as it was” — never an error, never a warning. This is now a confirmed-three-times bug shape in this codebase: MapBiomas Collection 10’s state/state_acronym rename map, and (2026-09-21) TWO separate places in ANEEL’s energy_generation migration — the eng column rename map in R/aneel.R and the dictionary’s ~variable matching column in R/dictionary.R both silently no-op’d for columns whose real post-clean_names() name had drifted from what the map’s keys assumed. A recode()/rename_with(recode, ...) call whose input keys were written against one snapshot of a source’s real column names is exactly as fragile as a sheet name or a required column — it needs the same live verification discipline (point 3 under “Investigating a broken or changed source” above), and probably deserves its own # FRAGILE: tag wherever it appears, not just a mental note.
  • The file-level download cache and the parsed-object cache in R/download.R are two independent mechanisms with two independent eligibility rules — a reason to exclude a source from one does not automatically apply to the other. Live incident (2026-09-21): ANEEL was excluded from the file-level disk cache (file_cache_get/file_cache_set, keyed on the raw downloaded bytes, no shared object, no mutation risk) — but the actual reasoning on record was about the parsed-object cache (parsed_cache_eligible(), a 1-slot cache of an already-fread()’d R object, excluded for .xlsx sources with real mutation risk under raw_data = TRUE). The two got conflated at some point, so every load_aneel() call re-downloaded a ~100MB file from scratch even back-to-back in the same R session, with no actual risk being guarded against. Before excluding a source from either cache, name which specific mechanism the risk applies to and check whether the same reasoning actually holds for the other one too — don’t assume “cache” is a single category just because both use that word.

Graduating a detect-only resolver: migrating the loader onto the real schema

Once a live check confirms the “different shape” assumption behind a detect-only resolver (previous section) — the file really did restructure, not just rename or bump a version — the loader (R/<source>.R) has to be rewritten to read the new layout before the resolver can start emitting a real url. Worked example: SEEG’s 2026-09-15 migration (R/seeg.R, actions/scrapers/resolve_seeg.R, tests/testthat/test-seeg-*.R) — a 250MB+ workbook, 5 sectors, old NIVEL 1..NIVEL 6 restructured into Setor de emissão/Categoria emissora/Sub-categoria emissora/Recorte/ Atividade geral.

  1. Extract cheap metadata once, cache it, never re-parse the full file per question. readxl::read_xlsx(file, range = readxl::cell_cols("A:I")) (or whatever span covers just the categorical columns, not the year columns) reads in seconds even on a 250MB+ workbook; save the result as an .rds under your scratch directory and answer every subsequent question — column names, distinct values, per-sector crosstabs — against that cached object. Do this for BOTH the old and new file so every mapping claim below is checked against real rows, not guessed from field names that merely sound similar.
  2. Rename columns by their real header text, never by position. readxl::read_xlsx() already returns the real header as the column name — use that directly (or rename via dplyr::rename(new = \Old Header`)) rather thannames(df) <- c(“a”, “b”, “c”, …)` against a guessed column order. A single miscounted or extra phantom column silently shifts every downstream field over by one and produces a wrong-but-not- obviously-wrong answer (a filter matching 0 rows is at least loud; a filter matching the WRONG column’s values usually isn’t). Caught twice during the SEEG migration this way — once from an extra guessed column, once from assuming the old file’s column order without checking it.
  3. Per sector (or whatever the natural unit of the source is), build a real crosstab, not an assumed mapping. count() every combination of the new file’s categorical fields for that sector, and separately for the old file’s equivalent fields, then read both outputs side by side to find the real correspondence from co-occurring values. Old and new labels are often NOT spelled identically at the same granularity (e.g. "Efluentes Liquidos" vs "Efluentes domésticos" may be different granularity, not just an accent difference) — this step is what catches that.
  4. Migrate smallest-to-largest, and verify each one fully before starting the next. Two passes per unit: (a) offline, against a small synthetic fixture that mirrors the real new-schema column layout (see any tests/testthat/test-seeg-*.R’s *_fixture() — full real year-column span, not a truncated one, or tidyselect range specs like x1970:x2024 will error on a fixture that only has 2 columns) with external_download() mocked; (b) live, against the real file, comparing exact row counts and reconciling totals across every geo_level the loader supports (municipality sum == state sum == country sum, for a fixed year). Don’t batch all units and verify once at the end — a bug caught in the smallest unit (fast to fix, fast to re-verify) is cheap; the same bug caught after 4 more units are built on the same broken assumption is not.
  5. Never merge two distinct source values into one output value. Grep the migrated code for case_when() and check every group_by()’s field list against the source’s real grain — a case_when() bucketing multiple new-schema values into one old-schema label, or a group_by() grouping on fewer fields than the previous step’s crosstab used, is silent granularity loss with no error to catch it. The correct move when a new-schema field has no clean 1:1 old-schema equivalent is a rename plus a straight value-for-value translation, not a bucketing chain.
  6. When a whole dimension is confirmed gone (not just relabeled), drop it and say so out loud at the time, not only in a code comment. A # FRAGILE: comment documenting exactly what was lost (which old column, what it used to let you split by) is necessary but not sufficient — tell the person you’re working with directly, in the moment, so a real data loss can’t hide behind a diff nobody reads line by line. SEEG’s biggest loss this way: seeg_land’s entire biome dimension and its full origin-to-destination land-cover transition matrix, collapsed into four coarser fields — surfaced explicitly before that sector was migrated, not after.
  7. Check any dictionary/vocabulary the new sector shares with already-migrated sectors for missing entries. A shared translation table (e.g. SEEG’s SEEG_EMISSION_TYPE_EN, covering the Emissão/Remoção/Bunker field every sector uses) built while migrating sector 1 may not cover a value that only sector 4 or 5 actually emits — confirmed live: seeg_land was the first sector to emit a plain "Remoção" value the dictionary didn’t have an entry for yet. A “translate every field, assert zero NA leaks” offline test (see any test-seeg-*.R) catches this immediately if the fixture happens to include that value — but a live run against the real file is what actually proves every REAL value the source emits is covered, since a synthetic fixture can only assert against values you already thought to include.

Verifying any change: capture first, then prove zero patches

Before changing anything about how a lookup resolves or the shape of the CSV, capture current behavior first — don’t trust that a refactor is behavior-preserving, prove it:

  1. Write (or extend) a script like data-raw/capture_resolution_matrix_v2.R (the current one — its predecessor, capture_resolution_matrix.R, is kept only for provenance and is no longer replayed, see test-resolution-matrix.R’s retirement note): query dataset_field() for every (survey, dataset, geo_level, year, field) combination that has a REAL row backing it, against the unmodified code and manifest. Save the answers to an .rds fixture under tests/testthat/fixtures/. Only query real keys — a blank-key query against a dataset that also has real override rows is not a valid query anymore (see above); if your capture script includes those anyway (easy to do by accident if it iterates whatever rows exist rather than filtering for “this dataset’s real key set”), your replay test needs to assert those specific entries now stop() instead of comparing values — see test-resolution-matrix-v2.R’s KNOWN_BASE_ROW_DATASETS handling for the pattern, born from exactly this mistake.
  2. Make your change.
  3. Assert the new code reproduces every captured real-key answer exactly — see tests/testthat/test-resolution-matrix-v2.R. Zero case_when patches. If reproducing the old answer needs a documented exception, that is a real regression to go fix, not a deviation to write a comment excusing. (The times this project needed patches — the original 5-tier migration, and later the base-row-deletion migration’s datasets_link() snapshot — every patch was a place the fixture and the new code legitimately disagreed on purpose, enumerated explicitly rather than absorbed into a blanket exception; see test-datasets_link.R’s delta list for the current one.)

Also re-run Rscript actions/scripts/build_manifest.R --dry-run twice in a row after any resolver or schema change: the second run must report Changed keys: 0. If it doesn’t, the change isn’t idempotent — that exact bug (a resolver “finding” a change that was already applied) is what originally motivated the self-sufficient-rows migration.

Investigating a broken or changed source

  1. Rscript actions/scripts/build_manifest.R --dry-run --check-all — probes every non-exempt URL in the manifest and reports failures without failing the run. Start here; it tells you what’s actually broken right now, not what you assume is broken.

  2. Open the URL in a browser. Read the page’s own JS/network tab before assuming you need to scrape HTML — most of this system’s working resolvers turned out to be reading a documented API the site’s own frontend already calls (see resolve_prodes.R’s header for the canonical example of finding this).

  3. A resolver finding the right URL is not the same as the package being able to read what’s at it. A resolver verifying a sheet name (and now a required column, see above) only proves the file exists and has the right shape at the header level — it says nothing about whether the treatment code that reads the DOWNLOADED file (R/prodes.R, R/mapbiomas.R, R/epe.R, …) can still parse it. A source can restructure a file’s contents — not just move where it lives — the same way it can restructure a page’s HTML: new column names, a new prefix convention on repeated columns, two previously-distinct columns colliding after a rename, a sheet that used to be long now wide. Live incident: MapBiomas’s Collection 10 migration moved every link correctly, but broke 4 real things inside mapbiomas_treat() that nobody had touched, 3 of them hard errors — the resolver-level verification had no way to catch any of them, because none of them are visible from a sheet name or a header row’s column names alone (a state/state_acronym collision, a window-column prefix change, a position-based extraction that silently broke when a column moved, an exact-name rename map that silently no-op’d). Whenever a resolver change is prompted by an upstream restructuring (not just a URL going stale), re-run the actual loader (load_<source>()) against the new file and check its output shape, not just that the resolver’s dry run exits clean. R/mapbiomas.R’s mapbiomas_treat() (and R/epe.R’s epe_energy_state_panel_treat()) tags every shape-dependent assumption in its own parsing code with a # FRAGILE: comment for exactly this reason — actions/scripts/fragility_notes.R’s collect_fragility_notes() greps the live file for these tags, once per source listed in that same file’s FRAGILITY_SOURCES table, and build_manifest.R lists the affected lines, by number, in the PR body whenever that source’s manifest row changes, so a reviewer knows what to re-check even when the resolver’s own diff looks like “just a URL.” If you add a new collection-sensitive assumption to a loader’s treatment code, tag it the same way rather than leaving it implicit — and if it’s a source not yet in FRAGILITY_SOURCES, add a row for it there too, or the tag won’t surface anywhere automated.

    A second, independent confirmation of this same lesson: ANEEL, 2026-09-21. R/aneel.R (already in FRAGILITY_SOURCES) had exactly the “resolver found the right URL, loader silently mis-reads what’s there” shape the MapBiomas incident above describes, on a source the resolver had never flagged as broken at all — found not by a resolver dry-run but by reviewing a migration (energy_generation moving off a dead GitLab xlsx onto ANEEL’s live CKAN CSV) against this checklist:

    • An exact-name rename map (dplyr::rename_with(dplyr::recode, ...)) silently no-op’d for ~12 keys and had no entry at all for ~15 more columns — the real post-clean_names() column names had drifted from what the map’s keys assumed, so those columns passed straight through unrenamed with zero error, in both the eng rename map AND a separate dictionary’s ~variable matching column (R/dictionary.R). dplyr::recode()’s unmatched-value/name behavior is “leave it exactly as it was,” never an error — this is now the THIRD confirmed live occurrence of this exact bug shape in this codebase (MapBiomas Collection 10’s state/state_acronym rename, and see the dplyr::recode R gotcha below), not a one-off.
    • An encoding assumption (fread(encoding = "Latin-1") + a compensating iconv(from = "ISO-8859-1")) was wrong, and had been since the source’s original 2023 commit — both files are genuinely UTF-8. Nobody had verified this at the byte level; see the new technique bullet under point 5 below for how it was actually confirmed.
    • A resource’s real content-type was assumed from stale code, not checked — energy_enterprises_distributed’s manifest URL now points at a ~106MB zip, but R/download.R hardcoded .csv for every ANEEL dataset. The unzip step never ran; every real download crashed. Same “a 200 response / matching sheet name is not enough” lesson as the rest of this section, just one layer earlier — the download dispatch itself was reading the wrong branch for that dataset’s real file type. None of these were things a resolver’s URL-probing or sheet/column check could have caught — the URL genuinely worked, returned real data, and validated fine at that layer. All three only surface by actually running the loader end to end against a real download and inspecting the output values, not just the output’s shape.

  4. If nothing serves the same data anymore and no narrower substitute is obviously correct, do not guess. Leave the row’s url as whatever it was (or blank it deliberately if it’s actively wrong), point docs_url at wherever a human should start looking, and write down exactly what you searched and ruled out in the resolver’s (or the row’s) nearest comment — resolve_epe.R’s energy_state_panel section was the precedent for a long time (see “Known limitations” below for how that specific case was later actually resolved, 2026-09-08 — the documented dead-end is what made the later fix fast, not wasted effort). This isn’t a permanent state: re-investigating the same site again later, especially after something else about it is already mapped, can turn up a page nobody had reason to check the first time.

  5. To check a real column header without downloading a multi-hundred-MB file, stream just the xlsx’s internal XML via HTTP range requests instead — xlsx is a zip, and both xl/workbook.xml (sheet names) and the target sheet’s own XML (header row) live well before the file’s central directory in practice. A small Python helper works for this: a file-like object whose read()/seek() issue Range: bytes=start-end requests instead of reading a local buffer, handed to zipfile.ZipFile. Needs seekable() returning True (an easy miss — zipfile checks for it) and a resolved r:id → sheet-file mapping via xl/workbook.xml + xl/_rels/workbook.xml.rels (sheets aren’t necessarily sheet1.xml in name order). Used this session to confirm the real header of Collection 9’s 606MB transition file in a few seconds instead of a multi-minute full download — this is purely an investigation tool for a human/session peeking at real shapes; it’s not what a resolver itself should do at runtime, since readxl can’t parse from a partial stream the way this ad-hoc reader can for a plain header check.

  6. To check whether a “mojibake” string is really the wrong encoding assumption (not just a rendering artifact), inspect the raw bytes directly — curl -r <start>-<end> <url> | xxd on the exact byte range containing the suspect character, compared against what that character’s real UTF-8 vs. Latin-1 encoding actually looks like at the byte level (e.g. “á” is 0xC3 0xA1 in genuine UTF-8; Latin-1 read as UTF-8 produces a visibly different, recognizably wrong byte pattern). Don’t trust a garbled string printed in a terminal or by R’s print() to diagnose which encoding is wrong — a string looks equally garbled whether the source is genuinely Latin-1 and being read as UTF-8, or genuinely UTF-8 and being read as Latin-1 (which is what actually happened with ANEEL, see the entry above — the source files were correct all along; fread()’s encoding argument was wrong, and had been since the source’s original 2023 commit, unverified). This is the string-encoding sibling of the ranged xlsx-header technique just above — same “verify the real bytes, don’t trust an assumption inherited from working code elsewhere in the file” posture.

The pipeline, end to end

actions/scripts/build_manifest.R [--dry-run] [--only src]... [--skip src]... [--check-all] [--no-watch]

  1. Reads the committed manifest AND the committed site-link inventory (actions/watch/site_links.csv — see “Site-link inventory watchers” below).
  2. Runs every registered resolver (resolve_<source>.R) inside tryCatch; one failure never touches another source’s rows.
  3. Merges each resolver’s output over the rows it owns. A brand-new row is seeded from the agreed value across its dataset’s existing sibling rows (not a base row — there isn’t one; see seed_new_row() in build_manifest.R) before the resolver’s own values are laid over it. A column the siblings disagree on seeds NA instead of a possibly-wrong value, forcing the resolver’s own value to win.
  4. Runs every registered watcher (watch_<source>.R) the same way — --only/--skip select by source name across both registries at once, --no-watch disables this pass entirely. Unlike a resolver, a watcher reports the FULL current link set it saw, so its output wholesale- replaces that source’s inventory rows rather than merging field-by-field.
  5. Re-sorts, then runs the full validation gate (actions/scripts/manifest_validate.R) against both the manifest candidate — validate_schema, validate_row_count (±10%), validate_no_deletions, validate_row_grouping, validate_dataset_level_agreement, validate_placeholders, validate_key_completeness, and (rows that changed only) validate_http — and the inventory candidate — validate_inventory.
  6. Writes a JSON report + the candidate manifest + candidate inventory to OUT_DIR (RUNNER_TEMP in CI, tempdir() locally). Never writes either committed path, under any condition.
  7. Exit codes (each now means “from a resolver, a watcher, OR a resolver’s own partial-sub-source failure — see point 5’s exception above”): 0 no changes · 10 changes present, needs a PR · 11 changes present AND something also failed — open the PR for the real changes anyway, and raise an issue for the failure, instead of the failure silently blocking the PR (this is what fixed the exact “mapbiomas failing blocks everyone else’s PR” incident this system used to have — see NEWS.md) · 20 validation failed · 30 something failed and there were no changes to report.

.github/workflows/update-manifest.yaml (Mondays 05:00 UTC + workflow_dispatch) runs this with no --skip flags (SEEG used to be skipped here; it no longer is — see Known limitations), and on exit 10/11: stages BOTH candidates onto their real paths, smoke-tests the manifest (devtools::load_all(); link_table()), then opens one PR via peter-evans/create-pull-request covering whichever changed — before the PR opens, not after. On exit 11/20/30 it also opens or reuses an issue, with the real resolver/watcher/validation failure messages in the body (not just a pointer at the step log). The candidate + report are always uploaded as a workflow artifact.

There is no auto-commit path anymore, for anything, ever. If you’re tempted to add one back “just for the safe cases” — don’t; that’s exactly the judgment call that turned into a recurring source of bugs and was deliberately removed.

Two Slack pings also ride alongside this flow now, purely informational — see “Slack notifications” below for what they are and why they never affect any of the exit-code behavior above.

Site-link inventory watchers

A second, parallel mechanism to resolvers, for sources whose data comes from scraping a page rather than a documented API: actions/scripts/site_inventory.R (generic fetch/normalize/diff/validate helpers) + actions/scrapers/watch_<source>.R (the actual per-page extraction logic, same auto-discovery convention as resolve_<source>.R) maintain actions/watch/site_links.csv — every download link a watched page currently advertises, diffed run over run.

This replaced an earlier design (still visible in git history) where resolve_mapbiomas.R scraped its own WordPress page and wrote a docs_url signal onto one manifest row when the site looked “ahead” of what the resolver found. That design had three structural problems a resolver-only system can’t avoid: it could only ever speak for one dataset, it couldn’t see a link disappearing (no candidate found was indistinguishable from “nothing new”), and comparing collection numbers like 10.1 vs 11 numerically assumed a labeling convention the source doesn’t actually owe anyone. An inventory fixes all three: it’s a plain diff of observed facts (link appeared / disappeared / moved), not a computed verdict, and it covers every link on the page, not just the ones a resolver’s config happens to ask about.

Identity for a row is (source, page, label, collection) — url is a VALUE under that identity, not part of it, so a moved link reads as one changed row instead of a delete-plus-unrelated-add. first_seen is set once and carried forward forever; there is deliberately no last_seen (it would change every run and turn this into a PR nobody reads).

Writing a watch_<source>.R mirrors writing a resolve_<source>.R (same “investigate live first, stop() on real failure, never guess” posture, same rows parameter shape — this source’s previously-committed inventory rows, so a watcher can compare “how many links did I see last time”), with one extra requirement: a scrape that finds nothing, or suspiciously fewer than last time, must never write — either failure mode would read as “the site deleted everything,” which is almost always wrong and would be the single worst thing this mechanism could get wrong. See watch_mapbiomas.R’s total-miss guard (zero links across every extraction strategy) and shrink guard (>50% drop in one run) for the pattern; both stop() rather than write a suspicious snapshot, and — being watcher failures — feed the same 11/30 exit-code path a resolver failure would.

Resolver verification caching

Verifying a Dataverse-style candidate means downloading the whole file — there’s no metadata API that exposes a workbook’s sheets or columns, only its checksum and size. That download is unavoidable the first time a given file is checked. What isn’t necessary is paying for it again every single scheduled run for a file whose verdict is already known — most weeks nothing upstream has changed, so a resolver that always re-derives from scratch is mostly re-confirming the same answer at real bandwidth cost.

actions/scripts/mapbiomas_resolver_cache.R (a committed CSV, actions/cache/mapbiomas_resolver_cache.csv) is the pattern for this: it records, per Dataverse file actually inspected, whether it passed and which sheet matched — keyed on (dataset, geo_level, file_id), but only ever trusted when two more things also match:

  • The file’s own checksum (Dataverse exposes this on the same dv_dataset_files() JSON call a resolver already makes to list a dataset’s files — no extra request). If the source ever replaces a file’s content under the same id, the checksum changes and the cached verdict is no longer trusted.
  • A fingerprint of the code’s own matching rules (sheet_pattern/required_col_pattern, hashed together). If a maintainer tightens either pattern later, every verdict computed under the old, looser rule is invalidated automatically — nobody has to remember to clear the cache by hand.

Why both, not just the checksum: a cache keyed on content alone would happily keep serving a “pass” verdict computed under rules that no longer apply, the moment someone edits required_col_pattern — exactly the kind of silent staleness this whole manifest system exists to prevent elsewhere (see “The one rule everything else follows from” at the top). Trusting a verdict requires both the thing being judged and the rule doing the judging to be provably unchanged since it was recorded.

Wiring it into a resolver: check the cache before the download, for every candidate the newest-first walk considers — a cached “pass” builds the result row directly (no download); a cached “fail” nexts to the older candidate exactly like a real check would; a miss (new file, changed checksum, or changed fingerprint) falls through to a real check, which then records its own verdict for next time. Cache updates are written to a candidate path and folded into the same PR-diff/exit-code machinery the manifest and site-link inventory already use — nothing about “the cache changed” is ever auto-committed either, matching every other rule in this file (see build_manifest.R’s cache_diff_n and mapbiomas_cache_changed side-channel). A run whose only change is a fresh cache entry still opens a small PR — a deliberate tradeoff (see that code’s own comment) rather than carving out a silent-auto-commit exception for “just this one safe case.”

Seeding and verifying: same posture as the site-link inventory — the first run after adding caching is necessarily cold (no committed cache to read yet, full download cost), its candidate gets hand-reviewed and committed as the seed, and every run after that should be warm. Prove the speedup is real, not just that the code compiles: run once cold, seed, run again warm, and diff the manifest output (not just check timing) — a cache hit has to resolve to exactly the row a full download-and-check would have produced. Live numbers from this pattern’s first build: 38 seconds warm against 2+ hours cold for ~10 MapBiomas configs. Also worth proving deliberately: temporarily set a config’s required_col_pattern to something no real file will ever satisfy, run it, and confirm the walk correctly exhausts every real candidate and reports nothing (not a crash, not a wrong value) rather than trusting this in theory — see R/mapbiomas.R’s treatment code fix and NEWS.md for the write-up of doing exactly this.

Slack notifications (informational side-channel, never gates anything)

Three Slack pings layered on top of the PR/issue mechanism above — they never change what fires, when, or whether a PR/issue opens. All three stay silent on any failure; failures always go through the issue path only, exactly as before this existed.

  • Watcher-changed: a watcher succeeds and finds a real inventory diff — fires alongside the PR that diff already opens, never instead of it. Also gated on validation having passed (length(errors) == 0), added after a live run caught the gap: a watcher can succeed and produce rows that validate_inventory() then rejects (see the SVG-markup live incident below), and without this gate the ping would fire for a diff that never actually became reviewable.
  • New-Dataverse-file-rejected: the resolver checksums a Dataverse file it’s never inspected before and the verdict is fail. Deliberately silent for a re-confirmed known fail (anti-noise, same reasoning as the inventory’s first_seen) and for a new file that passes (that already opens a real manifest PR — a second ping would be redundant). Note this does NOT mean “no PR opens” for that run — recording the rejection still writes a new row into the resolver cache, which still trips the routine cache-only PR the caching mechanism already opens on any new entry (see “Resolver verification caching” above); only the manifest CSV itself stays untouched. Get this distinction right in any message text — an earlier draft of this ping’s copy claimed “no PR was opened,” which was false.
  • PRODES/EPE new candidate failed content verification (2026-09-08): the same idea as the MapBiomas ping above, generalized instead of copied a second time — actions/scripts/resolver_alert_cache.R’s new_resolver_alerts(), a source-column-aware sibling of new_failed_files(). Fires when resolve_prodes.R’s .qml legend cross-check or resolve_epe.R’s per-block column checks reject a candidate they’ve never recorded before (or one whose previous recorded verdict wasn’t already fail — a pass-to-fail flip on the SAME key, e.g. the same PRODES stamp suddenly failing, is a genuine regression and alerts too, not just a brand-new key; found and fixed while verifying this feature, since keying “is this new” on identity alone — matching new_failed_files()’s file-checksum model too literally — silently missed it). Silent for a repeat of the exact same known fail, same anti-noise reasoning as the MapBiomas ping. Committed cache: actions/cache/resolver_alerts.csv, shared by both sources (no per-source file) so a future source can plug in as a FRAGILITY_SOURCES-style addition, not a new copy of the mechanism.

Mechanism: message bodies are composed in R (build_manifest.R) with jsonlite::toJSON() and handed to the workflow as ONE already-escaped line via GITHUB_OUTPUT, never re-parsed in bash. This is the deliberate fix for a real bug in the sibling datazoom_viz repo’s own Slack workflow: it builds a multi-line value with a bash heredoc containing real newlines, then interpolates it straight into a payload: | JSON string literal — breaks the instant there are 2+ items. Compose in R, escape with jsonlite, ship one line — don’t replicate the heredoc pattern for any future Slack message here.

Resolver instrumentation is purely additive. dv_file_layout() now records why it rejected a candidate via an enclosing layout_reason binding (<<- from inside the closure), reset at the top of every call — but every return(NULL)/next/return() decision in the walk is byte-identical to before this existed. If you’re touching this code and a change affects which candidate wins, that’s a different, much bigger change than what this feature is — verify with the same “capture first, then prove zero diff” discipline as any other resolver change.

Cache schema gained a reason column. read_resolver_cache() is now schema-tolerant — it fills any column the current code expects but an older committed CSV lacks with NA — so the committed cache never needs another manual migration when a future column gets added. Keep this permanently, not as a one-time shim.

Prerequisite: a SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL repo (or org) secret. The workflow steps are continue-on-error: true, so a missing/revoked secret can never turn a healthy run red — the pipeline’s actual pass/fail is driven only by build_manifest.R’s exit code, Slack delivery is never load-bearing.

Known limitations (don’t re-discover these from scratch)

  • COMEX onboarding (2026-10-17/18, branch update-comex, not yet merged) found load_br_trade() is broken in production right now, not just missing a resolver. The 4 manifest rows (export_mun, export_prod, import_mun, import_prod) had no resolver and a stale available_time (1997-2023); the real range, confirmed live across all 4, is 1997-2026 (the 2026 file is partial, rewritten monthly). A ncmv2/ folder mentioned in R/comex.R’s own comments (for import_prod) does NOT exist for any year 1995-2027, in either direction — a dead end, now documented in a comment so nobody re-investigates it. The real finding: balanca.economia.gov.br’s TLS certificate expired 2026-10-03 — load_br_trade() fails with an SSL error for every user (confirmed live on Windows, not just a CI/Linux problem). The live replacement is balanca.mdic.gov.br (same files, confirmed by size and Last-Modified), which is what the resolver and the manifest now point to — but it has its own problems: (a) its certificate chain is missing an intermediate, which Windows silently completes but OpenSSL/Linux (GitHub Actions) does not — a CI workflow step adding the missing intermediate to the trust store was added alongside the resolver so this doesn’t become a second weekly-noise case like SEEG; (b) its own certificate expires 2026-10-22 — outside this project’s control, worth rechecking if COMEX starts failing again after that date. Separately: this server returns HTTP 200 for literally everything, including a nonexistent year or the dead ncmv2/ path — a soft 404 (a ~1420-byte Joomla error page, text/plain) rather than a real one — so resolve_comex.R checks the real Content-Type (text/csv) via a single ranged GET per year, never the bare HTTP status. R/comex.R’s own column assumptions (co_ano, co_mes, co_pais, sg_uf_mun, co_mun, sh4/co_ncm, kg_liquido, vl_fob, plus the NCM-only sg_uf_ncm, co_via, co_unid, co_urf, qt_estat) were verified against real samples from 1997, 2025 and 2026 — all still match. Also fixed in the same change: R/comex.R’s own hardcoded dictionary URLs (NCM.csv, NCM_SH.csv) were still pointing at the dead host too — without this, the resolver fix alone would NOT have actually restored load_br_trade() for users (the main file downloads, but the dictionary join then fails). Found but deliberately NOT fixed here (separate task, documented as an Issue): the manifest’s baci_dic row points at the exact same dead host and file, with resolver blank — likely breaks load_baci() the same way (confirmed-equivalent on Windows, not yet confirmed on Linux).

  • SEEG’s resolver fails from GitHub Actions specifically (HTTP 403) but works from a normal connection. This is unrelated to SEEG’s detect-only status (below, now resolved) — it’s the live HTTPS download itself getting blocked, not a schema problem. The --skip seeg workaround no longer exists — it was removed from .github/workflows/update-manifest.yaml in commit cfe7d6f (“Re-enabled”). As of 2026-10-17, SEEG therefore runs every Monday in CI, fails, and posts a “Still failing” comment on Issue #344 each time. 2026-10-17 diagnostics (branch fix-seeg-resolver-diagnostics, not yet merged): SEEG’s edge is Amazon CloudFront, not Cloudflare as earlier guessed — a live 403 (no browser User-Agent) returns server: CloudFront, x-cache: Error from cloudfront, and AWS’s standard “ERROR: The request could not be satisfied … Request blocked” page, which AWS’s own docs describe as what CloudFront serves when an AWS WAF rule blocks the request (not confirmed which rule — an IP/hosting-range rule and a bot-detection rule render the identical page, so this is consistent with the IP/ASN-block hypothesis but doesn’t prove it). Confirmed NOT a missing-header issue: the same request succeeds from a non-CI connection with the identical headers. resolve_seeg.R now builds a detailed diagnostic into its stop() message on failure (status, URL, the handful of useful headers — server, cf-*/x-*, content-type/length, retry-after, location, via — cookie names only, the HTML <title>, and up to 600 chars of body, about 1.3 KB total; curl’s own error text is preserved when there is no HTTP response at all, e.g. a timeout or TLS reset — the original, lost 2026-10-06 patch didn’t handle that case). update-manifest.yaml was also fixed alongside it: the GitHub-issue-body Markdown rendering step used to mangle a multi-line diagnostic message with embedded HTML (evidence lines merged into one paragraph, the <title> text got interpreted as real HTML and stripped by GitHub) — now the detail goes into a properly-fenced code block (fence length chosen longer than any backtick run inside the body, so it can’t be closed early); single-line messages render byte-identical to before. Next step: merge this branch to master so the next scheduled Monday 05:00 UTC run posts real diagnostics on #344 instead of the old bare failure — not done yet, pending review.

  • SEEG graduated out of the detect-only category 2026-09-15 (see above) — same as IPS’s 2026-09-14 graduation. R/seeg.R’s five sectors were all rewritten against the real current schema and verified live.

  • epe/energy_state_panel HAD no working source — fixed 2026-09-08. (Historical note, kept because it’s the canonical worked example of the “investigate live, find nothing, leave docs_url pointing at where to start” pattern below — see point 4 of “Investigating a broken or changed source.”) The old Anuário chapter workbook 404’d with no replacement found at the time. A later re-investigation found the same BEN dashboard book national_energy_balance already reads has its own Chapter 8 page serving a working consolidated table — now resolved and automated (see resolve_epe.R’s header and NEWS.md). Sanity-checked against the real OLD source too (live via a git worktree at the pre-migration commit): 585 of 585 matched (year, fonte) cells for national_energy_balance came back an exact 0% delta — the only apparent mismatch turned out to be a one-year (2004) label inconsistency in the old hand-maintained workbook, not a data problem. Point worth generalizing: a dead link is not necessarily permanent — re-investigating the SAME site later, after something else about it has already been mapped (here, the BEN dashboard’s URL structure from national_energy_balance’s own fix), can turn up a page nobody had reason to check before.

  • Google Drive-hosted sources can’t be automated (IEMA, Imazon) — opaque Drive IDs, no discoverable version. SEEG’s and IPS’s actual files graduated off Drive links entirely (SEEG: a direct seeg.eco.br HTTPS URL; IPS: painel.ipsamazonia.org.br’s Strapi-hosted workbook) — this limitation no longer applies to either. SEEG’s separate per-gas-detail CSVs (gases.csv/ar2..6.csv, not currently read by R/seeg.R at all) remain Drive-hosted and still can’t be automated.

  • PRODES’s raster legend codes are hardcoded in R/prodes.R — INPE’s own encoding, not a URL token. resolve_prodes.R now cross-checks 5 of the 6 codes against the live .qml sidecar automatically on every run (2026-09-08, via actions/scripts/zip_remote_listing.R — a ranged-GET zip reader that recovers a small entry’s real content without downloading the whole archive), stop()ing if a label no longer matches. clouds = 99 is the one exception: no entry currently ships for it at all, so that specific code stays a documented, informational gap rather than a check that can ever pass — if PRODES ever adds it back, this becomes fully covered too. 2026-10-20: the codes live in ONE function, prodes_raster_code() in R/prodes.R; the resolver keeps its own copy at file scope (it runs without the package) and tests/testthat/test-prodes-resolver-legend.R fails if the two disagree — change both together. A zip without a .qml now fails the resolver (it used to skip the check with a message), every d<year>/r<year> entry is checked, and load_prodes() itself warns (prodes_check_qml()) when the .qml in the user’s own download disagrees. The codes stay hardcoded on purpose rather than read from the .qml at load time — see the comment above prodes_raster_code() for why.

  • zip_remote_listing.R must never pass useragent = NULL to curl::new_handle() — on curl 7.1.0 that sends no User-Agent header at all (verified 2026-10-20 against an echo server), and TerraBrasilis answers 404 to such requests. zip_remote_handle() sets the option only when a real value is given; use it for any new handle in that file.

  • The # FRAGILE: tag collector is generic (actions/scripts/fragility_notes.R, collect_fragility_notes(r_path, label)) — it used to be hardcoded to R/mapbiomas.R only (mapbiomas_fragility.R, sprintf("R/mapbiomas.R:%d", ...) baked into the format string), which meant tagging a shape-dependent assumption anywhere else got no automated PR-body surface. R/epe.R’s fonte_map, its " Do "/" De " capitalization fix, and its grupo != "Brasil" filter (see epe_energy_state_panel_treat()) are now tagged and picked up the same way R/mapbiomas.R’s tags are. Adding a new source is a row in FRAGILITY_SOURCES (same file) — changed_prefix, r_path, label, treat_fn — not a new wrapper file or a new block in build_manifest.R. A shape-dependent assumption in an R/*.R file that hasn’t adopted the tagging convention at all (or isn’t listed in FRAGILITY_SOURCES) is still only as durable as the comment next to it.

  • www.obt.inpe.br (DEGRAD) supports neither Range nor a useful HEAD — confirmed live (2026-10-06). A ranged GET returns Accept-Ranges: none and the full 200 response body instead of a 206, so zip_remote_entries() (the ranged-zip-listing technique resolve_prodes.R/resolve_baci.R rely on) can’t be used here without downloading the whole zip first. The obvious fallback, a plain HEAD request, is also broken on this host: it returns HTTP 200 with Content-Length: 0 and Content-Type: text/plain for all 10 DEGRAD-year URLs, so it can’t even confirm a file’s size. resolve_degrad.R’s degrad_peek_headers() works around both: it opens a real GET as a streaming curl connection, reads only the response headers, then closes the connection without ever consuming the body — giving a real Content-Length/Content-Type at near-zero transfer cost, with neither Range nor HEAD involved. DEGRAD is closed/historical (10 fixed year-rows, 2007-2016, will never grow), so this resolver only re-verifies existing manifest values against the live server rather than discovering new ones. If another source ever needs a resolver on this same obt.inpe.br domain, don’t assume Range or HEAD will work there either — re-test from scratch.

  • A merged fallback_notes value keeps silently re-using the fallback, with no further PR, until someone updates the resolver’s primary match. If a resolver recovers a value through its fallback_notes path (see point 5’s exception under “Writing a new resolver” above) and that PR gets merged WITHOUT also updating the resolver’s own primary-match table (e.g. resolve_deter.R’s slug_by_dataset), every later run finds the exact same value again via the same fallback, reports zero changes, and opens no PR — so the fallback_notes warning, visible only in that one merged PR’s body, that run’s workflow step summary, and that run’s JSON report, is easy to miss once the PR is old news. Confirmed live (2026-10-08) while building resolve_deter.R’s fallback: the PR body’s own checklist already tells the reviewer to update the primary table before merging, which is the actual fix for this — nothing further was added on top of that single warning. If this recurs in practice (a merged fallback left un-updated for a while), a cheap next step would be a Slack ping modeled on the existing ones (see “Slack notifications” above) that fires specifically when fallback_notes is non-empty on a run that reports zero changes — nobody has needed this yet.

  • load_deter()’s CRS was fixed 2026-10-09 (was: hardcoded polyconic, no datum/towgs84, biasing area). The projection choice never misaligned alerts and municipalities (both inputs are transformed through the same CRS from the same SIRGAS 2000/EPSG:4674 source), but the OLD +proj=poly ... +ellps=aust_SA string (near-identical to EPSG:5880 “SIRGAS 2000 / Brazil Polyconic,” general-purpose, not equal-area, with the ellipsoid additionally mistyped) made st_area() wrong, growing with distance from the projection’s central meridian (lon -54): against IBGE’s own official area-calculation projection (“Projeção Cônica Equivalente de Albers” — source: IBGE, “Malha Municipal Digital e Áreas Territoriais 2024,” Notas metodológicas 01/2025, Apêndice B), the old CRS’s measured bias was +0.45% for deter_amz, +0.85% for deter_cerrado, +0.14% for deter_pantanal, +0.51% for deter_non_forest, growing to roughly +5% for alerts west of -70°. load_deter() now uses that same Albers string directly (+proj=aea +lat_0=-12 +lon_0=-54 +lat_1=-2 +lat_2=-22 +x_0=5000000 +y_0=10000000 +ellps=GRS80) — verified live against two independent references (lwgeom’s ellipsoidal geodesic area, a Lambert azimuthal equal-area projection): median ratio 1.00000, 98% of rows within ±0.001%. R/degrad.R had the IDENTICAL wrong string at its own operation_crs call site — fixed 2026-10-12, see the entry below. The newer named EPSG codes for this same projection (10856/10857, “SIRGAS 2000 / Brazil Albers,” registered 2025-05-16) resolve to NA silently (no error, no warning) on a representative install (PROJ 9.3.1, sf 1.0.19) — that’s why the fix uses the explicit proj4 string, not the named EPSG code; re-test before ever switching to it. Separately, a small number of raw alerts have no row at all after the municipality st_intersection() — this moved slightly with the CRS change (boundary slivers differ by projection): 16 of deter_amz’s 461,071, 6 of deter_cerrado’s 134,165 (was 7 under the old CRS), 2 of deter_pantanal’s 24,155, 0 of deter_non_forest’s — cause not investigated, numbers small enough not to block anything so far, but worth knowing before trusting a raw-vs-treated row count match exactly; compare by alert_id, not row count.

  • load_degrad()’s CRS fixed 2026-10-12 (same bug as DETER’s above) — and, 2026-10-16, the 2 bugs found while verifying it (tracked upstream, in the sibling package, in datazoompuc/datazoom.amazonia#350, related to the already-open #283) are now ALSO fixed, via one unified change. operation_crs had the identical +proj=poly ... +ellps=aust_SA string as DETER’s; replaced 2026-10-12 with the same IBGE Albers projection.

    Then, 2026-10-16: a new harmonize_degrad_year_crs() is applied to every year’s raw geometry, right after download and before bind_rows() (and after the raw_data = TRUE early return, so that path stays genuinely unharmonized — see below), transforming it via sf::st_transform() to a single real, PROJ-registered CRS — SIRGAS 2000, EPSG:4674, the CRS 2015-2016 already use — instead of the old post-bind_rows() block that only ever handled the “missing CRS” case. This closes both #350 bugs at once, as a natural consequence of using a real target CRS instead of two separate fixes:

    1. A time_period crossing a raw-CRS group boundary no longer crashes. The 3 previously-failing ranges (2009:2010, 2014:2015, 2007:2016) all succeed now — verified live: row count and total km² for each equal the exact sum of loading every year separately (231,453 rows / 145,554.45 km² for 2007:2016), every geometry valid and non-empty, sf::st_crs() of the merged result is EPSG:4674, and 2010:2012 (inside one group) is unchanged. Still tracked, separately, as #283.
    2. The SAD69→SIRGAS 2000 datum shift is now really applied. Measured directly against the raw files: 2007-2014 polygons move 59.5-75.0 m (median 65-69 m depending on year); 2015-2016 move 0.0 m (already SIRGAS2000). The real source of the shift turned out to be the TOWGS84 embedded in the 2010-2014 files’ own BOUNDCRS (matching the pre-existing fallback string used for 2007-2009), not the separately registered EPSG:4618 operation (which agrees to within 0.3 m) — the # FRAGILE: tag was corrected accordingly.

    Effect of the datum shift alone (current code vs. the 2026-10-12 Albers-only code, same projection, same downloads): total area over 10 years +0.0009% (-0.0001% to +0.0026% per year, 2015-2016 exactly 0; corrected 2026-10-17 – an earlier draft of this note and of the commit message below had the sign flipped); municipality-level area delta median 0.004-0.1%, 95th percentile 1.2-2.2%, with outliers up to ~15% in 2011 on municipalities that only have 1.5-4 km² of DEGRAD that year (a fixed metric shift reads as a large percentage on a tiny area); row count after st_intersection() changes by -14 to +3 per year (-36 of 231,489 over 10 years); 7 municipality-year pairs appear/disappear, all tiny slivers (0.00002-0.017 km², 0.031 km² total over 10 years).

    Combined effect of both fixes vs. the ORIGINAL polyconic code (unchanged from the 2026-10-12 measurement for the area-bias figures — a translation doesn’t change area): +0.41% total area bias (+0.30% to +0.74% by year; by longitude, up to +4.8% west of -70°, smallest — +0.06% — between -55 and -50); 231,453 output rows for 227,218 raw polygons (net +1.9%), vs. 231,483 under the original code. New code’s area matches an independent geodesic reference and a Lambert equal-area projection to within ±0.00001 (1st-99th percentile), every year.

    raw_data = TRUE is unaffected — verified byte-identical to the pre-2026-10-16 code on 2010:2012, 2007:2009, 2015:2016 and 2010:2014 (harmonization runs after that early return, so it still returns each year’s genuinely original per-year CRS, including the NA/SAD69/SIRGAS2000 mix). DETER is unaffected throughout (its own raw files are already SIRGAS 2000).

    A separate, pre-existing data limitation surfaced (not introduced) by this fix: 2007-2009’s raw shapefiles have no view_date column at all, so a multi-year load spanning those years now returns NA in date/data for 2007-2009 rows instead of crashing — same column-selection shape as DETER’s alert_type gap above. Not a bug in this fix, just newly visible now that cross-group loads actually complete; documented in NEWS.md as user-facing.

    Status, 2026-10-17: the CRS/datum fix itself is committed and pushed (commit 52bcc7d on update-degrad, not yet merged to master — note its message contains “closes #350”, so merging this branch as-is will auto-close the issue regardless of the test-coverage status below; that’s fine once both are ready, but don’t merge before then if the issue should stay open a while longer). tests/testthat/test-degrad-crs.R was added (3 synthetic-fixture tests / 18 expectations, no network, ~1.2s — fails on the pre-fix code, passes on the fix) and check_all_loads.R’s TIME_PERIOD_BY_FN$load_degrad was widened from 2016 alone to c(2009, 2010, 2016) (crosses both raw-CRS group boundaries against the real INPE servers, ~75s, fails on the pre-fix code) — both verified (full suite: 602 expectations, 0 failures) but, as of this writing, not yet committed; a second commit for these two files is prepared and pending.

  • TerraBrasilis has no English-language file for DETER/PRODES — confirmed live, 2026-10-10 (meeting task 6). The catalog’s PT/EN entries are catalog-metadata only: every PT/EN pair (68 GeoNetwork-UUID-matched groups, cross-checked again with a UUID-free pass across all 116 EN / 115 PT entries in the live /business/api/v1/download/all catalog) shares the exact same underlying link — including all 4 DETER products load_deter() reads and the PRODES raster load_prodes() reads. The download API’s own OpenAPI spec (/business/v2/api-docs) exposes no language parameter at all, and ?lang=, ?language=, ?locale=, and Accept-Language were all tested against both the catalog endpoint and a real DETER Pantanal download — byte-identical response every time (same zip member hashes). Column headers are therefore fixed per product regardless of the catalog’s display language: DETER Pantanal/non-forest and the PRODES vector shapefile are already English-named internally (UUID, CLASS_NAME, AREA_KM, … — dBASE’s 10-char field-name limit truncates a couple, e.g. CREATE_DAT), DETER Amazônia/Cerrado mix English technical names with Portuguese abbreviations (AREAUCKM, MUNICIPALI, GEOCODIBGE, UF, UC), and the PRODES raster load_prodes() actually reads has no attribute table at all (just .tif + a GRASS .txt report + a .qml legend, the legend itself holding 3 Portuguese labels). Conclusion: downloading “in English” from the source isn’t a real option for either package — R/deter.R’s existing hand-written dplyr::rename() (only 2 of DETER’s raw columns ever reach load_deter()’s output: view_date→date/data, classname→alert_type/tipo_de_alerta; everything else is dropped by the select()) is already the minimal correct approach. No code change made for this task.

  • A separate, real gap found during that same check: alert_type VALUES stay in Portuguese even when language = "eng". load_deter() renames the column but never recodes the values inside it, and the raw values aren’t even consistent across the 4 products: upper-snake Portuguese (DESMATAMENTO_CR, CICATRIZ_DE_QUEIMADA, …) for deter_amz, only DESMATAMENTO_CR for deter_cerrado, and accented lowercase Portuguese transliterated to ASCII (e.g. supressao com solo exposto) for deter_pantanal/deter_non_forest. Not one of the meeting’s 6 tasks and not yet scoped — a real fix would need a cross-product value dictionary (3 different vocabularies to reconcile) plus a decision on what to do with an unrecognized label, similar in shape to SEEG’s SEEG_EMISSION_TYPE_EN dictionary (see “Graduating a detect-only resolver” above).

Finishing activation (the system exists but has never run on its own)
